questions.q: Which HPV viral protein is utilized to form virus-like particles (VLPs) in prophylactic HPV vaccines?
questions.exp: The L1 protein is the major capsid protein encoded by the Late (L) region of the HPV genome. It has the ability to self-assemble into virus-like particles (VLPs), which form the basis of prophylactic HPV vaccines.

questions.q: A 6-year-old child from Bihar presents with prolonged fever, massive hepatosplenomegaly, and progressive diffuse ashy-gray hyperpigmentation of the face and abdomen. Which Leishmania species is most likely responsible for this clinical presentation?
questions.exp: The clinical features of visceral leishmaniasis (hepatosplenomegaly, fever) with characteristic diffuse hyperpigmentation giving the name 'Kala-azar' (Black Sickness) in Bihar, India, is caused by Leishmania donovani, which is anthroponotic in the Indian subcontinent.

questions.q: A 35-year-old meat handler presents with multiple verrucous papules on his hands. Which HPV type is most likely responsible for this occupational dermatosis?
questions.exp: HPV 7 is specifically associated with butcher's warts, an occupational dermatosis seen in meat handlers. It is a low-risk cutaneous HPV type belonging to the α genus.

questions.q: A patient develops permanent depigmentation following cryotherapy for a viral wart, but there is no evidence of scarring. Which principle of cryosensitivity best explains this outcome?
opts: Keratinocytes are destroyed at higher temperatures than melanocytes
Fibroblasts are more sensitive to cold than melanocytes
Melanocytes require temperatures of -30°C to -35°C for destruction
Melanocytes are destroyed at -4°C to -7°C while fibroblasts survive until -30°C to -35°C
questions.exp: Melanocytes are the most cryosensitive cells, undergoing destruction at just -4°C to -7°C, while fibroblasts (responsible for collagen/scar formation) are most resistant and survive until -30°C to -35°C. This differential sensitivity explains why hypopigmentation commonly occurs before scarring in cryotherapy.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman develops recurrent painful ulcerations around her ankles with subsequent porcelain-white stellate scars. Histopathology shows fibrin deposition and hyalinization of dermal vessel walls without significant inflammatory infiltrate. What is the correct pathophysiological classification of this condition?
questions.exp: This describes livedoid vasculopathy (atrophie blanche), which is a chronic thrombo-occlusive disease rather than a true vasculitis. It primarily affects young to middle-aged women on distal lower extremities and is characterized by segmental hyalinizing changes in vessel walls with fibrin deposition.

questions.q: A patient presents with suspected post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis following a recent episode of impetigo. Which serological test combination provides the highest diagnostic yield for confirming preceding streptococcal skin infection?
opts: ASO titre combined with anti-DNase B
C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate
questions.exp: ASO response is weak in streptococcal skin infections, whereas anti-DNase B is more reliably elevated. Testing both ASO and anti-DNase B together yields a positive result in 95% of patients evaluated for post-streptococcal sequelae.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with skin thickening limited to her fingers and face, along with a 15-year history of Raynaud's phenomenon. She also has difficulty swallowing solid foods and multiple small dilated blood vessels on her face. Which autoantibody is most likely to be positive in this patient?
questions.exp: This patient has features of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc), previously known as CREST syndrome (Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia). Anti-centromere antibody is characteristically associated with lcSSc, while anti-Scl-70 is more commonly seen in diffuse cutaneous SSc.

questions.q: A 7-year-old girl presents with a solitary, rock-hard, mobile nodule on her right cheek that has been slowly growing for 6 months. Histopathology reveals a well-circumscribed dermal tumor with peripheral basophilic cells showing frequent mitoses and central anucleate eosinophilic cells with retained cellular outlines. Which genetic mutation is most commonly associated with this tumor?
questions.exp: The clinical and histopathological features are classic for pilomatricoma. Approximately 75% of pilomatricomas harbor activating mutations in the CTNNB1 gene encoding β-catenin, which stabilizes the protein and leads to unchecked proliferation of hair matrix cells via the Wnt signaling pathway.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with recurrent pneumonia (4 episodes in the past year), persistent oral thrush despite treatment, and an unusual infection with Pneumocystis jirovecii. According to the SPUR criteria for suspecting primary immunodeficiency, which feature is NOT part of this warning sign mnemonic?
opts: Recurrent infections of the same type
questions.exp: SPUR stands for Serious, Persistent, Unusual, and Recurrent infections - the warning signs for primary immunodeficiency. Periodic fever syndromes, while important in immunology, are not part of the SPUR criteria.

questions.q: A 45-year-old HIV-positive male presents with violaceous nodules on the lower extremities. Biopsy shows spindle cells forming vascular slits. Immunohistochemistry is most likely to show strong positivity for which of the following lymphatic endothelial markers?
questions.exp: Kaposi sarcoma spindle cells express a lymphatic endothelial phenotype with strong positivity for markers such as podoplanin (D2-40), PROX1, LYVE-1, and VEGFR-3. KSHV infection reprograms blood vascular endothelial cells toward this lymphatic phenotype.

questions.q: Which mechanism best explains why high-risk HPV types (16, 18) cause malignancy while low-risk types (6, 11) typically cause benign lesions?
opts: High-risk HPV DNA remains as extrachromosomal episome maintaining E2 function
High-risk HPV integration disrupts E2 gene leading to constitutive E6/E7 expression
Low-risk HPV E6 protein has stronger binding affinity to p53
High-risk HPV types exclusively infect basal keratinocytes
questions.exp: In high-risk HPV, viral DNA integrates into the host genome causing disruption of the E2 gene. Loss of E2 repression leads to uncontrolled E6 and E7 oncogene expression, resulting in p53 degradation and pRb inactivation respectively, driving carcinogenesis.

questions.q: Keratins are obligate heteropolymers requiring co-expression of paired proteins for functional filament formation. Which chromosomal locations harbor the Type I and Type II keratin gene clusters respectively?
questions.exp: Type I (acidic) keratins are located on chromosome 17q21, while Type II (basic-to-neutral) keratins are located on chromosome 12q13. Functional keratin filaments require one member from each family to form heterodimers.

questions.q: A 4-year-old child presents with widespread flaccid bullae and superficial skin denudation. A frozen section of the peeled skin roof is performed. Which histopathological finding would confirm the diagnosis of Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome over Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis?
opts: Full-thickness epidermal necrosis with subepidermal split
Cleavage at the level of stratum granulosum with acantholytic cells
Interface dermatitis with apoptotic keratinocytes at the basal layer
Suprabasal acantholysis with tombstoning of basal cells
questions.exp: In SSSS, the cleavage occurs superficially within or just below the stratum granulosum, showing acantholytic cells with minimal inflammation. In contrast, TEN demonstrates full-thickness epidermal necrosis with a subepidermal split.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with asymmetric, irregular, branching violaceous discoloration on her lower extremities and trunk that does not completely resolve upon warming. She has a history of recurrent spontaneous abortions. Which underlying condition is most strongly associated with this clinical presentation?
questions.exp: The patient has livedo racemosa (asymmetric, irregular, persistent pattern) with recurrent pregnancy loss, which is a hallmark presentation of Antiphospholipid Antibody Syndrome (APLS). LRC is present in 25% of primary APLS and up to 70% of SLE-associated APLS cases, serving as a predictor for multisystem thrombosis.

questions.q: A 62-year-old uncircumcised man presents with a glistening, reddish-orange plaque on the glans penis with symmetrical involvement of the inner prepuce. On dermoscopy, pinpoint purpuric spots are noted. Biopsy shows epidermal atrophy with lozenge-shaped keratinocytes and a dense band-like plasma cell infiltrate. What is the definitive treatment for this condition?
questions.exp: This clinical and histological picture is classic for Zoon's balanitis. While topical therapies provide temporary relief, circumcision is the gold standard curative treatment as it eliminates the occlusive foreskin environment essential for disease pathogenesis.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man from Brazil presents with progressive nasal congestion, epistaxis, and a collapsed nasal bridge 3 years after a healed cutaneous ulcer on his arm. Biopsy shows sparse parasites with intense granulomatous inflammation. Which immunological mechanism best explains this destructive mucosal disease?
opts: Specific T-cell anergy with parasite tolerance
Hyperergic Th1 response with excessive TNF-alpha production
Predominant Th2 response with IL-4 and IL-10
Defective macrophage activation with uncontrolled parasite multiplication
questions.exp: Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis (MCL) is driven by an exaggerated Th1 hyperergic response with massive TNF-alpha production, causing intense host tissue destruction despite sparse parasites. This is the pathophysiological opposite of DCL, which is characterized by T-cell anergy.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man undergoes cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen for a biopsy-proven superficial basal cell carcinoma on his back. Which freeze-thaw protocol is most appropriate for this lesion?
opts: Single freeze-thaw cycle with rapid thaw
Single freeze-thaw cycle with slow thaw
Double freeze-thaw cycle with rapid thaw
Double freeze-thaw cycle with slow thaw
questions.exp: For malignant lesions like basal cell carcinoma, a double freeze-thaw cycle is recommended as the first cycle impairs circulation and increases tissue conductivity, allowing deeper penetration during the second freeze. Slow thawing maximizes cellular destruction through prolonged hypotonic exposure and ice recrystallization.

questions.q: A 28-year-old man presents with mild dysuria and scanty clear urethral discharge for 2 weeks. He was treated with azithromycin 1g single dose but symptoms persisted. Urethral swab NAAT is positive for an organism with a single-base mutation in the 23S rRNA gene. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.exp: Mycoplasma genitalium is increasingly recognized for treatment failures due to rapidly emerging macrolide (azithromycin) resistance, which is mediated by a single-base mutation in the 23S rRNA gene. It is the second most common cause of NGU after Chlamydia.

questions.q: A 68-year-old male on dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + clopidogrel) for recent coronary stent placement requires excision of a basal cell carcinoma on the nose. According to current guidelines for antithrombotic therapy in dermatosurgery, what is the most appropriate perioperative management?
opts: Discontinue both agents 7 days before surgery
Continue aspirin, discontinue clopidogrel 5 days before surgery after cardiology clearance
Continue both agents and proceed with surgery using meticulous hemostasis
Bridge with low molecular weight heparin after stopping both agents
questions.exp: Current guidelines recommend continuing antithrombotic therapy for cutaneous surgery as the bleeding risk is manageable with local hemostatic measures, while discontinuation significantly increases thromboembolic risk, especially within 6 months of coronary stent placement. Meticulous hemostasis with electrocautery, pressure, and topical agents is preferred over drug cessation.

questions.q: A 32-year-old man presents with multiple firm subcutaneous nodules on his scalp and upper extremities. Biopsy of one lesion shows shadow (ghost) cells with dystrophic calcification and foreign body giant cell reaction. Which syndrome should be most strongly considered in this patient?
questions.exp: Multiple pilomatricomas should raise suspicion for underlying genetic syndromes. Gardner syndrome (familial adenomatous polyposis) is a key association where multiple pilomatricomas or epidermoid cysts with pilomatricoma-like changes serve as cutaneous markers. Other associations include myotonic dystrophy, Turner syndrome, and Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome.

questions.q: A 3-week-old premature neonate in the NICU receiving total parenteral nutrition with lipid infusions develops fungemia. Blood cultures grow a yeast that can be subcultured on Sabouraud's dextrose agar without lipid supplementation. Which Malassezia species is most likely responsible?
questions.exp: Malassezia pachydermatis is the only non-lipid-dependent (nonobligatory lipophilic) species in the genus and is known to cause nosocomial bloodstream infections in premature neonates receiving parenteral lipid infusions. Its ability to grow without lipid supplementation distinguishes it from other Malassezia species.

questions.q: A 2-year-old child presents with widespread blistering since birth, particularly affecting palms and soles. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in the helix termination motif of the keratin rod domain. Which of the following best explains the severe phenotype in this patient?
opts: Disruption of disulfide bond formation in hair keratins
Impaired keratin intermediate filament assembly and elongation
Defective glycine-serine rich head domain interactions
Abnormal keratin expression switching from K8/K18 to K5/K14
questions.exp: The helix initiation and helix termination motifs at the ends of the rod domain are highly conserved and play a pivotal role in keratin intermediate filament assembly and elongation. Mutations in these 'hot spots' often lead to more severe phenotypes in inherited keratin disorders such as epidermolysis bullosa simplex.

questions.q: A 22-year-old man presents with asymptomatic hypopigmented macules on his upper back. KOH examination shows short hyphae and round spores. What is the mechanism responsible for the hypopigmentation in this condition?
opts: Direct melanocyte destruction by fungal toxins
Competitive inhibition of tyrosinase by azelaic acid
Blockade of melanosome transfer to keratinocytes
questions.exp: In Pityriasis Versicolor, fungal lipases break down skin surface lipids into dicarboxylic acids, particularly azelaic acid. Azelaic acid competitively inhibits tyrosinase, the key enzyme in melanin synthesis, leading to decreased melanin production and clinical hypopigmentation.

questions.q: A 38-year-old man presents with rapidly progressive skin thickening involving his trunk, arms, and legs over 6 months. Compared to limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis, which internal organ complication is he at significantly higher risk of developing?
questions.exp: Diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (dcSSc) is characterized by widespread skin involvement extending proximal to elbows/knees and trunk. Patients with dcSSc are at significantly higher risk for early severe organ involvement including scleroderma renal crisis and pulmonary fibrosis, compared to limited cutaneous SSc.

questions.q: An 8-year-old boy has had 3 episodes of bacterial meningitis in 2 years, requiring hospitalization and intravenous antibiotics each time. Which component of the SPUR criteria does this presentation BEST exemplify?
questions.exp: Serious infections in SPUR criteria refer to infections requiring intravenous antibiotics or hospitalization, such as bacterial meningitis, sepsis, or deep-seated abscesses. This case primarily demonstrates the 'Serious' component of primary immunodeficiency warning signs.

questions.q: Which viral gene product of HHV-8 drives cell cycle progression by inhibiting the retinoblastoma tumor suppressor protein (pRb)?
questions.exp: vCyclin (ORF 72) is a viral homolog of cellular cyclin D that inhibits pRb, allowing infected cells to bypass G1 arrest and progress to S phase. LANA-1 maintains latency, vFLIP provides anti-apoptotic effects, and vGPCR activates angiogenic signaling pathways.

questions.q: During removal of an epidermoid cyst on the back, the surgeon notes that the cyst wall has ruptured with spillage of keratin contents. What is the most critical step to prevent recurrence?
opts: Irrigate the cavity with povidone-iodine solution
Completely excise the remaining cyst wall and epithelial lining
Pack the cavity with antibiotic-soaked gauze
Close the wound primarily without any further intervention
questions.exp: Recurrence of epidermoid cysts occurs due to retained epithelial lining that continues to produce keratin. Complete removal of all cyst wall remnants is essential even after rupture. Simple irrigation or primary closure without complete excision leaves epithelium behind, leading to recurrence.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman is diagnosed with cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 3. Molecular analysis reveals integration of HPV DNA into the host genome. Which viral proteins are primarily responsible for the oncogenic transformation by inactivating tumor suppressor proteins p53 and pRb respectively?
questions.exp: The oncogenic potential of high-risk HPV types is mediated by E6 and E7 proteins. E6 inactivates the tumor suppressor p53, while E7 inhibits the retinoblastoma protein (pRb), leading to disruption of cell cycle control and cellular immortalization.

questions.q: Which histopathological finding is characteristic of Zoon's balanitis?
opts: Munro microabscesses in the stratum corneum
Corps ronds and grains in the epidermis
questions.exp: Zoon's balanitis characteristically shows lozenge or diamond-shaped keratinocytes separated by uniform intercellular spaces described as 'watery spongiosis,' along with epidermal atrophy, loss of rete ridges, and a dense subepidermal plasma cell infiltrate with hemosiderin deposition.

questions.q: A 32-year-old man who has sex with men presents with intense dysuria, mild urethral discharge, and bilateral conjunctivitis. He reports recent insertive oral sex. Which pathogen is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.exp: Adenovirus accounts for 2-4% of NGU cases and is classically associated with intense dysuria and concurrent conjunctivitis. It is detected more frequently among MSM, often linked to insertive oral sex.
